title: Concatenated Words
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive splitting versus a trie-shared word-break dynamic programming approach.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of distinct words, return all words in the array that are concatenated words, meaning a word that can be entirely formed by concatenating at least two shorter words from the same array.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: A word is concatenated exactly when its characters can be partitioned into two or more pieces, each of which is itself a word present in the array (the same word used as a whole is not itself a valid single "piece" since at least two pieces are required). This is precisely the word-break problem, applied independently to each word using the full word list as the dictionary.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking If a Long Compound Name Is Built From Shorter Names on a Roster
blocks.text: Picture checking whether a long compound name is entirely built by joining two or more shorter names already present on a roster. Marking which prefix lengths of the compound name are reachable using roster names, moving left to right, answers whether the FULL compound name is reachable using at least two names.

blocks.caption: A word is concatenated if it splits into two or more pieces, each a word from the same list

blocks.text: Result: ["catsdogcats","dogcatsdog","ratcatdogcat"]. "catsdogcats" splits into "cats"+"dog"+"cats". "dogcatsdog" splits into "dog"+"cats"+"dog". "ratcatdogcat" splits into "rat"+"cat"+"dog"+"cat".

Before recursively trying every possible way to split each word into pieces (an exponential search without memoization), notice that this is exactly the classic word-break dynamic programming problem: a boolean reachability array over prefix lengths, filled in using a dictionary of the OTHER words.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A word of length n can be checked for splittability using a boolean array dp of size n+1, where dp[i] means the prefix of length i is reachable via some sequence of dictionary words.

Observation 2: dp[0] is trivially true (an empty prefix needs no pieces). For each reachable dp[i], checking every dictionary word starting at position i extends reachability to dp[i + word length] if that substring matches a dictionary word.

Observation 3: The word matches the "at least two pieces" requirement automatically, AS LONG AS the single piece spanning the ENTIRE word (from position 0 to n) is excluded from counting as a valid completion by itself.

Observation 4: Building a TRIE from all words lets each dp[i] extend to matches directly by walking the trie forward from position i, rather than re-slicing and re-hashing every possible substring starting there, sharing structure across all the different starting points and words checked.
This leads to building a trie from all words once, then running a word-break style DP per word (walking the trie from each reachable prefix length), excluding the whole-word-as-one-piece case.
For each word, recursively try every way to split it into pieces, checking each piece against a hash set of words, without memoization.
Why the code is written this way

items: Recursively trying every split point directly implements the definition.
Without memoization, the same starting position gets recomputed repeatedly across different branches, costing exponential time in the worst case.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to word length) worst case per word without memoization.
Space: O(word length) recursion depth.
Limitation: a word-break DP over prefix reachability, combined with a shared trie for prefix matching, brings this down to a low-order polynomial per word.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a trie from ALL words once. For each word, run a word-break DP: dp[0] = true. For each i where dp[i] is true, walk the trie starting at position i, character by character; whenever the walk passes an end-of-word marker at some position j, set dp[j] = true (UNLESS i is 0 and j is the very end of the word, which would mean using the entire word as a single piece, not allowed). The word is concatenated exactly when dp[word length] ends up true.
Build a shared trie once; run a word-break DP per word using trie walks, excluding the single whole-word piece case.

blocks.content: {"headers":["dp index reached","Trie walk from there","New dp index set"],"rows":[["dp[0] = true","Walk \"cat\", hits end-of-word at position 3 (not the whole word since word length is 6)","dp[3] = true"],["dp[3] = true","Walk \"dog\" from position 3, hits end-of-word at position 6","dp[6] = true, MATCH (dp[word length] is true)"]]}

blocks.text: The dp array correctly tracks every prefix length reachable via some sequence of dictionary words, and building it via trie walks (rather than re-slicing and re-hashing substrings) shares the character-matching work across every different starting position and word checked. Excluding the case where a single piece spans the ENTIRE word correctly enforces the "at least two pieces" requirement, since only genuinely SHORTER intermediate pieces are allowed to mark dp positions before the very end.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total characters times average word length) considering all words and their trie walks.
Space: O(total characters) for the trie.

blocks.text: Concatenated Words combines the classic word-break dynamic programming pattern with a shared trie, applied independently to every word in the list using the rest of the list as its dictionary.

items: Forgetting to exclude the whole word as a single piece, which would incorrectly mark every word as "concatenated" from itself.
Rebuilding a fresh dictionary structure per word instead of sharing one trie built once from all words.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "this is word-break, applied per word, using the rest of the list as the dictionary, with at least two pieces required" connects this problem immediately to a very well known pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can this string be built by joining other strings from the same list", think: word-break dynamic programming, using a shared trie for efficient prefix matching.

items: How would you also RECONSTRUCT one valid split (the actual list of pieces), not just determine whether a word is concatenated?
Word Break and Word Break II, the foundational versions of this same dynamic programming pattern.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^word length) worst case per word; the trie plus word-break DP approach costs roughly O(total characters times average word length), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: word-break dynamic programming, applied per word, sharing a single trie across the whole word list.
Core Idea: a word is concatenated exactly when its prefix-reachability array reaches the full length using at least two dictionary pieces.
Time: O(2^word length) per word for the brute force, O(total characters times average word length) for the trie-DP approach.
Space: O(word length) for the brute force, O(total characters) for the trie-DP approach.
Most Important Observation: excluding the whole-word-as-one-piece case is the only twist distinguishing this from plain word-break.
Interview Difficulty: a hard word-break variant combined with trie-based prefix matching.
One line memory trick: word-break per word, excluding the single whole-word piece.
